intro: Every Rust-specific word, tool and acronym used in the basic track, with a short definition. Linked words in the lessons point here; hover them to see the definition in place.

terms.definition: Two or more names (variables, references, pointers) that give access to the same piece of memory. Garbage-collected languages alias freely; Rust allows it only for read-only access.

The core borrowing rule: at any moment a value may have either any number of shared references (`&T`) or exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`), never both. It rules out data races and iterator invalidation at compile time.

An operation that is occasionally expensive but cheap on average over many calls. `Vec::push` sometimes reallocates and copies every element, but because capacity doubles each time, the total cost stays proportional to the number of pushes.
A popular crate for application error handling. `anyhow::Result<T>` holds any error, like `Box<dyn Error>`, and lets you attach context messages with `.context()` / `.with_context()`.
A fixed-size sequence of `N` elements of type `T`, stored inline with no heap allocation. The length is part of the type, so `[u8; 4]` and `[u8; 5]` are different types.

The primitive conversion operator, e.g. `300u32 as u8`. It never fails: integer casts keep the low bits (truncation) and float-to-int casts saturate. Prefer `into()` and `try_from()` when you do not want silent truncation.
A function defined in an `impl` block that has no `self` receiver, called with `Type::name()`. The equivalent of a static method; `new` constructors are associated functions by convention.
Metadata attached to an item with `#[...]` (or to the whole crate with `#![...]`). Examples: `#[derive(Debug)]`, `#[test]`, `#[error("...")]`. Attributes drive the compiler, lints and macros.
A name attached to a value, introduced by `let`, a function parameter or a pattern. Bindings are immutable unless declared with `mut`.
Accessing a value through a reference without taking ownership of it. The owner keeps the value; the borrow ends at the reference's last use.

The part of the compiler that verifies, on MIR, that every reference is valid for as long as it is used and that the aliasing XOR mutability rule holds. It runs at compile time only and leaves nothing behind at runtime.
Verifying that an index is within the length of an array, slice or `Vec` before accessing it. Rust always checks indexing and panics on an out-of-range index instead of reading neighbouring memory.
An owning pointer to a value allocated on the heap. When the box is dropped, the heap value is dropped and its memory freed. The simplest smart pointer.

A heap-allocated value of any type that implements `std::error::Error`. The `?` operator converts any error (and `&str` messages) into it, which makes it a convenient catch-all error type for applications and `main`.
An ordered map from `std::collections`, implemented as a B-tree. Keys are kept sorted and must implement `Ord`; use it instead of `HashMap` when you need sorted iteration or range queries.
How many elements a `Vec` (or bytes a `String`) can hold before it must allocate a bigger buffer. Always at least the length; `Vec::with_capacity(n)` reserves it up front.
Rust's build system and package manager: it creates projects, resolves and downloads dependencies, compiles, runs tests, builds documentation and publishes crates. You rarely invoke `rustc` directly.
The file Cargo writes with the exact version of every dependency used in a build, so that builds are reproducible. The equivalent of `package-lock.json`.
The TOML manifest of a Cargo package: its name, version, edition, dependencies, features and build profiles.
Rust's character type: one Unicode scalar value, always 4 bytes. It is not a byte and not a UTF-16 code unit; a string's `char`s come from decoding its UTF-8 bytes.
The official linter, run with `cargo clippy`. It ships hundreds of lints that catch common mistakes and suggest more idiomatic code.
The trait for explicit duplication: `.clone()` produces an independent copy of a value, allocating and copying heap data if needed (a deep copy for `String` and `Vec`).

An anonymous function that can capture variables from its surrounding scope, written `|args| body`. Closures are passed to combinators like `map` and `and_then`; they are covered in depth in the intermediate track.
A method that transforms or chains values without explicit control flow, such as `map`, `and_then`, `ok_or` and `unwrap_or` on `Option` and `Result`.
A named compile-time constant, e.g. `const MAX: u32 = 5;`. Its type must be written, its value must be computable at compile time, and it is inlined at every use.
A function that can be evaluated at compile time, and therefore called in the initializer of a `const` or `static`.

A marker trait for types that are duplicated bit by bit on assignment instead of moved: integers, floats, `bool`, `char`, shared references, and tuples or arrays of `Copy` types. A type that owns a resource can never be `Copy`.

Rust's unit of compilation and distribution: a library or a binary, compiled as a whole from a root file (`lib.rs` or `main.rs`) and its modules. Third-party crates are what other ecosystems call packages or libraries.
The public registry of Rust crates. `cargo add` and the `[dependencies]` section of `Cargo.toml` fetch from it by default.
A reference or pointer to memory that has already been freed or reused. In safe Rust it cannot exist: the compiler rejects any reference that would outlive the value it points to.
Two threads accessing the same memory at the same time, at least one of them writing, without synchronization. The result is undefined behaviour; safe Rust rules data races out at compile time.
The formatting trait for developer-facing output, used by `{:?}` and `{:#?}`. It is usually generated with `#[derive(Debug)]`.
An automatic conversion the compiler applies to references, e.g. `&String` to `&str` and `&Vec<T>` to `&[T]`. It is why functions that take `&str` or `&[T]` accept owned types too.
The `#[derive(...)]` attribute asks the compiler to generate a standard implementation of traits such as `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq` or `Hash` for a struct or enum.
Using a pattern to take a struct, tuple, array or enum apart and bind its pieces to names, e.g. `let (x, y) = point;` or `Point { x, .. }`.
The hidden integer stored in an enum value that records which variant it holds. `match` reads it to choose the arm; niche optimization can hide it inside the payload.
The formatting trait for user-facing output, used by `{}` in `println!` and `format!`. It is never derived: you implement it by hand to choose the wording.

An expression that never produces a value because control flow leaves: `return`, `break`, `continue`, `panic!` or an infinite `loop`. Its type is `!` (never), which fits anywhere; the `else` block of `let else` must diverge.
Freeing the same allocation twice, which corrupts the allocator and is undefined behaviour. Move semantics prevent it: after a move, only the new owner will free the value.

Running a value's cleanup when its owner goes out of scope: freeing heap memory, closing files, releasing locks. Types customise it by implementing the `Drop` trait; `std::mem::drop(x)` drops a value early.
A hidden boolean the compiler keeps on the stack when a value is only moved on some paths, so that it knows at the end of the scope whether it still has to drop it.

Choosing which method implementation to call at runtime, through a table of function pointers (a vtable) stored next to the data pointer. In Rust it only happens when you ask for it with `dyn Trait`; ordinary method calls are resolved at compile time (static dispatch).
A named language revision (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) chosen per crate in `Cargo.toml`. Editions batch the rare breaking syntax changes, while crates on different editions still link together.
`HashMap::entry(key)` returns a handle to a slot that may or may not be occupied, so that "insert if missing, then update" needs a single lookup: `*map.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1`.
A type whose value is exactly one of several variants, each of which may carry its own data. Rust enums are sum types, not just named integer constants.
The standard interface for error types. It requires `Debug` and `Display` and optionally exposes an underlying cause through `source()`.
A compiler analysis (used by Go and the JVM) that detects values outliving their function and silently moves them to the heap. Rust has no such step: it rejects the dangling reference instead.

The guarantee that a `match` covers every possible value of the matched type. A missing case is a compile error, so adding an enum variant points you to every match that must handle it. Guards are not counted.
Code that evaluates to a value. In Rust blocks, `if`, `match` and `loop` are expressions; a trailing semicolon turns an expression into a statement, whose value is `()`.
A pointer that carries extra data next to the address: a length for slices and `&str`, a vtable pointer for `dyn Trait`. It takes two words, 16 bytes on 64-bit targets.
The mechanism to call functions written in other languages (usually C) and to be called by them. It requires `unsafe` and is covered in the advanced track.
Traits for infallible conversions. Implementing `From<A> for B` also gives `Into<B> for A`. The `?` operator calls `From::from` on errors; `TryFrom` / `TryInto` are the fallible counterparts.
A runtime component that periodically finds unreachable objects and frees them, as in Java, Go, Python and JavaScript. Rust has none: memory is freed deterministically when its owner is dropped.
Code parameterized over types, such as `Vec<T>` or `fn largest<T: Ord>(...)`. Rust compiles generics by monomorphization; they are covered in depth in the intermediate track.

What a reader perceives as a single character, which may be made of several Unicode scalar values (an emoji with a skin-tone modifier, a letter plus a combining accent). The standard library does not segment graphemes; use a crate such as `unicode-segmentation`.
An `if condition` after a pattern in a `match` arm: the arm runs only if the pattern matches and the condition is true. Guards are not considered for exhaustiveness.
A denial-of-service attack that sends many keys crafted to land in the same hash bucket, turning a hash map's O(1) operations into O(n). Rust's default hasher is randomized to resist it.

The algorithm that turns a key into a hash for `HashMap`. The default, SipHash 1-3 with a random seed, favours resistance to hash flooding over raw speed; faster hashers such as `ahash` or `rustc-hash` can be plugged in.
The standard hash table from `std::collections`. Keys must implement `Eq` and `Hash`; lookups return `Option<&V>`, and iteration order is unspecified.
Memory allocated at runtime, for data whose size or lifetime is not known at compile time. In Rust every heap allocation has an owner (a `Box`, `Vec`, `String`...) that frees it when dropped.
Runs a block only when a value matches one pattern, binding its parts: `if let Some(x) = value { ... }`. A shorter `match` with a single interesting arm.

A block that attaches behaviour to a type: methods and associated functions (`impl Type { ... }`) or a trait implementation (`impl Trait for Type { ... }`). Data and behaviour are declared separately.
The trait a `for` loop calls on what you give it. `for x in &v`, `for x in &mut v` and `for x in v` use three different implementations, yielding `&T`, `&mut T` and `T`.
A value that produces a sequence of items through repeated `next()` calls, implementing the `Iterator` trait. Adapters such as `map`, `filter` and `sum` are lazy and compile to plain loops.

Modifying a collection while iterating over it, so that the iterator points into a buffer that has moved or changed. Java detects it at runtime, C++ leaves it undefined; in Rust it is a borrow error at compile time.
A compiler that turns bytecode into machine code while the program runs, as in the JVM or V8. Rust compiles ahead of time, so there is no JIT and no warm-up.
`let PATTERN = value else { ... };` binds the pattern's variables in the current scope, or runs the `else` block, which must diverge, when the pattern does not match. The idiomatic guard clause.
The region of code during which a reference is valid. The compiler infers most lifetimes; when it cannot, you name them with annotations like `'a`. The topic of a lesson in the intermediate track.
The compiler backend, shared with Clang and Swift, that `rustc` uses to optimize code and generate machine code for each target.
Code that writes code at compile time. Calls end with `!` (`println!`, `vec!`, `format!`) and are expanded before type checking, which is how format strings get checked against their arguments.
Compares a value against patterns from top to bottom and runs the first arm that matches. It is an expression, and it must be exhaustive.
One `pattern => expression` branch of a `match`. Arms are tried from top to bottom and the first matching one runs; an arm that can never match is reported as unreachable.
A function defined in an `impl` block whose first parameter is a receiver (`self`, `&self` or `&mut self`), called with dot syntax: `r.area()` is `Rectangle::area(&r)`.
A simplified, control-flow-graph form of your program that `rustc` builds after type checking. The borrow checker and drop insertion run on MIR, before it is lowered to LLVM.

A namespace inside a crate, declared with `mod name`. Module declarations tell the compiler which files belong to the crate; visibility (`pub`) is controlled per module. Covered in the intermediate track.
Compiling a separate copy of generic code for each concrete type it is used with, so `Vec<i32>` and `Vec<String>` become independent machine code. Zero cost at runtime, more work at compile time.
Transferring ownership of a value by assignment, argument passing or returning. Only the stack part is copied bit by bit; the source becomes unusable, which the compiler checks statically.
The keyword that makes a binding (`let mut x`) or a reference (`&mut x`) mutable. Without it, a binding and everything reachable through it is immutable.
A reference that allows modifying the borrowed value. While it is alive no other reference to the same value may exist, so it is also called an exclusive reference.
A tuple struct with a single field, such as `struct Meters(f64);`, used to give a distinct type to an existing one. It has the same memory layout as the wrapped type, so it is free at runtime.
Storing an enum's tag in bit patterns its payload can never have. Because a reference is never null, `Option<&T>` uses the null pointer for `None` and is the same size as `&T`.
The borrow checker rule, default since Rust 2018, that a borrow lasts until its last use rather than until the end of the enclosing block. Reordering code is often enough to fix a borrow error.
An LLVM annotation promising that no other pointer accesses the same memory, which enables extra optimizations. Rust can emit it for every `&mut T`; in C you must promise it by hand with `restrict`.
The standard enum for a value that may be absent: `Some(T)` or `None`. It replaces null, and you must handle `None` before you can use the inner value.

An arithmetic result that does not fit in the integer type. Rust panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds; `wrapping_*`, `checked_*`, `saturating_*` and `overflowing_*` methods make the behaviour explicit.

Rust's memory model: every value has exactly one owner, a variable or a field; ownership can be moved; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. The compiler enforces these rules, with no runtime cost.

The reaction to a bug or a broken invariant: the current thread stops, normally by unwinding the stack. An uncaught panic in the main thread ends the process with exit code 101. Panics are not exceptions and are not meant for control flow.

A description of the shape of a value, used to test and destructure it: literals, ranges, `Some(x)`, `Point { x, .. }`, `[first, .., last]`, `A | B`, `n @ 1..=9`. Patterns appear in `match`, `let`, `if let`, function parameters and `for`.
A named set of compiler settings in Cargo. `dev` (debug) builds fast with overflow checks; `release` (`--release`) optimizes fully and removes overflow checks. Benchmark only release builds.

Applied to a `Result` or an `Option`, it unwraps the success value or returns early from the function with the error (converted through `From`) or `None`. It only works inside functions that return a compatible type.

The idiom, from C++, of tying a resource to an object's lifetime: acquire it when the value is created, release it in its destructor. In Rust every owned value follows it, and ownership guarantees the release happens exactly once.
A reference-counted smart pointer: several `Rc` handles share ownership of one heap value, which is dropped when the last handle goes away. Single-threaded; covered in the intermediate track.
Replacing a full buffer with a bigger one: allocate, move the elements, free the old buffer. Any pointer into the old buffer becomes dangling, which is why references into a `Vec` block `push`.
The first parameter of a method, which says what the method does with the value: `&self` reads it, `&mut self` modifies it, `self` consumes it.
A non-owning pointer to a value, created with `&` or `&mut`. It is a plain machine pointer, guaranteed by the compiler to be non-null and to point to a live value.
The three streams of Rust toolchains. A new stable release ships every six weeks; nightly carries unstable features behind flags.
The standard enum for an operation that can fail: `Ok(T)` with the value or `Err(E)` with the error. Recoverable failures are returned as values and visible in the signature.
The support code a language needs while a program runs: garbage collector, scheduler, JIT, reflection. Rust's runtime is tiny: a startup routine, the allocator and the panic machinery.
The official Rust language server. Through the Language Server Protocol (LSP) it gives any editor completion, go-to-definition, inline types and diagnostics.
The Rust compiler. It compiles one crate at a time, parsing, type checking, borrow checking and handing optimized code to LLVM. Cargo calls it for you.
The official code formatter, run with `cargo fmt`. It applies one canonical style, so formatting is never a code-review topic.
The toolchain installer and manager: it installs and updates `rustc`, `cargo`, the standard library and tools for each release channel and target.
The region of code, usually a `{ ... }` block, where a binding is valid. When an owner goes out of scope, its value is dropped; locals are dropped in reverse order of declaration.
Inside an `impl` block or trait, an alias for the type being implemented: `fn new() -> Self`.
Declaring a new binding with the same name as an existing one, possibly of a different type. The old value is hidden, not mutated: useful for parse-and-refine steps.
A read-only reference. Any number of shared references to a value can exist at the same time, and they are `Copy`.
A borrowed view of a contiguous run of elements owned by an array, a `Vec` or another slice. It is a fat pointer: address plus length.
A type that acts like a pointer but adds ownership semantics or bookkeeping, such as `Box` (unique owner), `Rc` (reference-counted shared owner) or `String`. Covered in the intermediate track.
The per-thread memory region where function calls keep their local variables. Allocation is a pointer bump and values are freed when the function returns; their size must be known at compile time.
A global value with a single fixed address for the whole run of the program, e.g. `static GREETING: &str = "hello";`. `static mut` exists, but every access needs `unsafe`.
The lifetime of data that lives for the whole program, such as string literals stored in the binary. `&'static str` is the type of a string literal.

The library that ships with every toolchain: collections (`Vec`, `HashMap`), strings, I/O, threads, `Option`, `Result` and the core traits. It is precompiled for each target and linked statically into your binary.
A borrowed view of UTF-8 text: a pointer and a length in bytes. String literals are `&'static str`; a `&String` coerces to `&str`, so prefer `&str` for parameters.
An owned, growable, heap-allocated UTF-8 string: internally a `Vec<u8>` guaranteed to hold valid UTF-8. It cannot be indexed by integer.
Text written in quotes in the source, like `"hello"`. Its bytes are embedded in the read-only data of the binary and it has type `&'static str`: no allocation, valid for the whole program.
A type that groups named fields, e.g. `struct User { name: String, age: u32 }`. It has no hidden header, no inheritance and no identity beyond its bytes.
A type whose values are exactly one of several alternatives, with a tag recording which one. Rust enums are sum types; structs and tuples are product types.
The platform you compile for, named by a triple such as `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` or `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. `rustup target add` installs the standard library for cross-compiling.
A popular crate that generates the `Display`, `Error` and `From` implementations of a library's error enum from attributes such as `#[error("...")]` and `#[from]`.
The set of tools for one Rust version and target: `rustc`, `cargo`, the precompiled standard library, `clippy`, `rustfmt` and friends. `rustup` installs and switches between toolchains.
A named set of methods that types can implement, similar to an interface. `Display`, `Clone`, `Copy` and `Drop` are traits; they are the topic of the first lesson of the intermediate track.
A fixed-size group of values of possibly different types, e.g. `(i32, f64, &str)`, accessed with `.0`, `.1` or destructuring.
A struct with positional rather than named fields: `struct Color(u8, u8, u8);`. With a single field it is called a newtype.
The `::<T>` syntax that supplies generic type arguments to a function call, e.g. `"12".parse::<i64>()`, when inference has nothing else to go on.

The binary encoding of signed integers used by every modern CPU: the top bit has a negative weight, so in `i8` the bits `1000_0000` mean -128. Casting between `i8` and `u8` reinterprets the same bits.
The compiler phase that verifies every expression has a consistent type and resolves traits and methods. In `rustc` it runs before borrow checking, so type errors are reported first.
The compiler deducing types you did not write, from how values are used later in the same function. Function signatures are never inferred.
An operation the language gives no meaning to, such as reading freed memory or a data race; the compiler may assume it never happens, so anything can result. Safe Rust has no undefined behaviour.
Any Unicode code point except the surrogate range used by UTF-16. It is exactly what a Rust `char` holds; `.chars()` iterates over them.
The empty tuple `()`, the type of "no meaningful value", similar to `void`. Statements, functions without a return type and blocks ending in `;` evaluate to `()`.
A struct with no fields, `struct Marker;`. It takes zero bytes and is used as a type-level marker.

A keyword that unlocks operations the compiler cannot verify, such as dereferencing raw pointers or accessing a `static mut`. Inside it, upholding Rust's rules is your job. Covered in the advanced track.

What a panic does by default: walk back up the stack of the current thread, dropping every live value, so files are closed and locks released. With `panic = "abort"` the process stops immediately instead.
Methods on `Option` and `Result` that return the inner value or panic on `None` / `Err`. `expect("why")` adds a message. Fine in tests and prototypes, a code smell elsewhere.
Accessing memory after it has been freed, a classic source of crashes and security holes in C and C++. In safe Rust the borrow checker makes it impossible.
Unsigned and signed integers as wide as a pointer (64 bits on 64-bit targets). Lengths and indexes are always `usize`.
A Unicode encoding using 2 or 4 bytes per character, used internally by JavaScript, Java and Windows strings. Characters outside the basic plane take two units, so `"🦀".length` is 2 in JavaScript.
A variable-width Unicode encoding using 1 to 4 bytes per character, compatible with ASCII. All Rust strings are UTF-8, which is why they cannot be indexed by integer in O(1).
One of the alternatives of an enum, e.g. `Message::Quit` or `Some(x)`. A variant may carry no data, a tuple or named fields.
A growable array on the heap: three words on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) owning a buffer of `T`. When it is full, `push` reallocates to double the capacity.
A program that executes bytecode instead of native machine code, such as the JVM or the Python interpreter. Rust programs compile to native code and need no VM.
`_` matches any single value without binding it; `..` ignores the remaining fields or elements. A `_` arm makes a `match` exhaustive but also hides future variants.
An abstraction that compiles to the same machine code you would write by hand, so you pay nothing at runtime for using it: iterators, generics, newtypes, `Option<&T>`.
